demo-1-on-a-development-node-alice-and-b.text: Demo 1 on a development node: Alice and Bob run a registry from the release archive.

As a Cardano developer who knows cardano-cli, wallets, faucets and Koios but has never used Singular, you want to see the whole of Demo 1 work before you spend test ada: a registry is created, a key is inserted, changed, terminated and taken over by a new owner of the name, and every refusal appears where the page says it will. This page does that on a private development node that the archive starts for you. Every command is copied as it stands; nothing in it needs a faucet, an account or a checkout.

When it works, you have read sixteen receipts, each the one JSON document a singular registry or open-datum command prints, and you have seen two wallets sign in the two ways Singular offers. The same steps on the public preprod network, with the faucet and Koios, are on the preprod runbook. Read this page first if you want to see it run for nothing; read the runbook when you are ready to spend test ada.

the-story.text: Alice boots a registry whose application is open datum: a key's live value is an output at the application's script, holding the key's one active token under an inline envelope. The envelope has a protected part (this registry, its active policy, the key, the controller and a protected deposit) and a free payload. Only the controller may replace the payload. A termination does not release the key's custody to its controller: the registry takes it in and donates it to the treasury, less the declared tip.

An insert or a terminate books and stops: its request waits at the registry, and its receipt names the request and the deadline by which it must be folded. The fold is its own command, open-datum fold, run by whichever wallet folds. Each step below is a separate process and prints one JSON receipt. The saved state directory carries the identity from one process to the next.
Alice and Bob keep no signing key on disk, and the story shows both ways to sign:

Alice signs from her vault, in one command. She names the vault file and the descriptor her passphrase is read from. The command builds the run's one bundle of transactions, signs it from the vault, sends it and prints its receipt once every transaction has landed.

Bob signs the external way. His write names his wallet's address and a new bundle file. The command builds its whole run as that one bundle, signs nothing, sends nothing and exits with status 19, the outcome waiting-for-signatures. He then signs the bundle from his vault with singular wallet sign and sends it with singular submit. Until submit finds the bundle's transactions on chain, the command's own fields (the request, the fold, the root) are only what the bundle expects, and the receipt says so under expected.

what-you-need.text: A Linux machine with Nix and flakes enabled, plus git, jq and curl. The quickest way to the programs is the Nix shell of singular-demo, described in the next section; it needs only Nix and curl.

This archive, downloaded, checked and extracted. The onboarding page gives the download, the checksum check and the extraction commands. Every command below runs from the extracted directory, the one that holds DEMO1.md and onchain/.
Time. Building from source compiles a large Haskell stack unless the public binary cache serves it; see the next section. A binary install that needs no Nix is coming in issue 695.

build-the-commands.text: The quick way: the shell. From the extracted archive's directory,

opens a shell with singular, open-datum, the development node devnet and jq on the path, all built by the project's CI. With the caches accepted it builds only the shell itself and fetches about 190 MiB instead of compiling the Haskell stack. Its limits: it is pinned to release v0.12.0, it is built for x86_64 Linux only, it needs Nix, and it keeps the development node's files in one directory per user, so run one node at a time (on a multi-user Nix install a user outside trusted-users cannot take the caches from a flake; the shell's README says what to change). In that shell, name the programs like this and skip the build below; everything after it runs as written:

The shell's own $blueprint holds the same bytes as onchain/plutus.json, the archive's file, but it sits in the Nix store with no version.txt beside it, and singular registry describe (step 2) refuses a blueprint without one, so keep the archive's file as blueprint.

The other way: build from the archive. This suits another release or another system. Nix reads a flake from a Git tree, and the application's flake reaches the registry's sources one directory up, so the extracted archive must be made into a Git tree first. This commits nothing and contacts nothing. Nix then warns that the tree is dirty; that is expected.

The project's public binary cache holds both executables for x86_64-linux, so a build that finds them downloads about 100 MiB each instead of compiling. Add the cache before the first build, either with the two settings below on the command line, or in /etc/nix/nix.conf as extra-substituters and extra-trusted-public-keys if your user is not trusted by the Nix daemon:

The flakes also name the Cardano build cache https://cache.iog.io; Nix asks once whether to accept it. No release yet ships ready-built binaries (that is planned in issue 348). singular --version prints the program, its version and the commit it was built from; a build that carries no commit says commit unknown, and the path the build prints then tells which build you hold.

start-one-development-node.text: The development node is private and generated: a fresh chain whose genesis funds the addresses you name. Alice and Bob each make a wallet with singular wallet create: a vault, a file that holds the wallet's signing key sealed by a passphrase, which a script supplies on an inherited file descriptor (typed at a prompt when you run it by hand). The node is given the printed addresses and never sees a key, and it funds nothing outside itself. Alice books, and Bob folds. Each wallet is funded with one output, and nothing is split.
The node is a Koios-shaped HTTP endpoint at providerUrl. The same commands run against the preprod Koios on the runbook page with only these three settings changed.

run-the-story.text: First the two payloads the story uses and the helpers the later steps call. A payload is Plutus data in the detailed JSON schema; these two are a one-entry map from the bytes of name to the bytes of alice and of bob.
When you are done, stop the node with kill "$devnet_pid".

Run the fold of a request before the deadline its booking's receipt names (foldDeadline); a later fold is refused by open-datum, naming the deadline, before anything is signed. Giving open-datum insert or open-datum terminate the --fold switch books and folds in one command, with one wallet: with the external signer the one bundle then holds the booking and the fold, and one signing covers both; with the vault the one command signs and sends both.

A write that is refused before it builds anything (the retired reject, a closed registry's update, a terminal key) writes no bundle. While a bundle waits for its signatures, the same wallet's next write of that registry stops with the same outcome, waiting-for-signatures, naming the waiting bundle, and builds nothing. singular wallet sign refuses a bundle whose signers do not include the vault's address, and singular submit sends only the transactions the chain does not hold, so it can be run again on a bundle that has landed. A wrong passphrase or an unreadable vault is refused, naming the vault, before the blueprint, the provider or the state directory is read. A vault run whose answer is lost leaves its bundle pending, its fields under expected, and the next write of that wallet stops on it like any waiting bundle.
--key is the key as text, its UTF-8 bytes (616c696365 is alice). --key-hex 616c696365 names that key too, which is how a key that is not printable text is given. A key is 1 to 32 bytes either way.

insert builds the key's envelope around the payload: constructor 0 over the control and the payload, the control being constructor 0 over the version 1, the registry's state asset (its state policy and token name, as the create receipt prints them in pins.pinState and token), the active policy (pins.pinActive), the key, the controller's payment key hash (the signing wallet's, which the create receipt prints as walletKeyHash) and the protected deposit in lovelace. The deposit is 2 000 000 when --deposit is not given; --deposit LOVELACE names another amount, and one below 2 000 000 is refused. That minimum is the client's own policy: the chain checks only that a request's deposit equals the control's at booking and that an update keeps at least the control's deposit, and sets no floor. The insert receipt and the preview receipt print the envelope it built.

what-you-should-see.text: open-datum create prints the state token (stateToken), the seed, the token, the pins (the applied open-datum script, the state script and the three witness policies) and the published reference outputs. The preview names the token and the seed before anything is submitted. The wallet holds one output, so no seed is given: the registry boots from the change of its first publication. create also needs two values that have no default: --registration-cost LOVELACE, the cost each registration of the registry pays, in lovelace, zero or more, and --booking-width MS, the widest validity interval a registration booking may carry, in positive integer milliseconds; the runs on this page pass 0 and 60 000, and the registry fixes both for its life. create writes no identity file. Every later command derives the registry from the state token and this archive's blueprint, checks it against the chain and refuses by name when they disagree, such as state-token-not-found or registry-pin-mismatch application. Its receipt carries the describe command the next step runs, printed as describeCommand.

singular registry describe reads the registry page with the command the create receipt printed (describeCommand, run as printed): which registry this is, which release it runs, what its rules are and what it holds now. The page shows the public history of the state token from create to the live state output, read through the named provider, whose answers nothing here verifies; the release label is the archive's own claim, and the page is unsigned.

open-datum insert books the insertion through the application: its receipt names the pending request (request), the booking's transaction, the envelope kept for the fold and foldDeadline, the time and the slot by which the fold must happen. Nothing is folded, and the registry's root and your saved state do not move.

open-datum fold stages the fold of the pending requests with the wallet whose address it is given, which need not be the wallet that booked. It settles every request that passes, up to nine, each settled key's one active token landing in an output at the application, carrying its envelope inline. Its receipt names, under expected, each settled request, its key, its edge and the output it delivered in the settled list, beside the fold's transaction, the new root and how many milliseconds remained before the deadline, and lists the requests it left out in excluded.

open-datum inspect reads the key active, with the holding, its envelope and payload, the registry's root and its separately observed tip. The reads behind a write are not guaranteed to come from one chain state.
open-datum update replaces only the payload. The receipt's root equals the root before it.
open-datum inspect shows the new payload, the same control and deposit, and the same root.

open-datum terminate books the termination against the live holding: its receipt names the pending request, the custody output the booking spends into it, the protected deposit and the lovelace it transfers into the request.

open-datum fold stages and, once sent, lands its fold: the token is burned and the custody is donated to the treasury, less the declared tip. None of the custody is paid back to the controller. Its receipt states the donation.
open-datum inspect reads the key terminal, with no holding.

singular registry reject is retired. The registry's state script refuses a spend with the rejected action, so the command refuses by name (exit 10, outcome client-refusal) before it reads, signs or submits anything, and writes no bundle. A request nobody folded stays pending until its owner takes it back with singular registry reclaim, after its processing deadline and while its retract window is open.
open-datum insert stages a new request, which the registry takes once the late one is reclaimed.
open-datum fold folds it, and the key reads active.

singular registry reclaim takes back a new pending insertion that nobody folded, inside its retract window. An earlier attempt is refused, naming when it opens; another wallet is refused as not the request's owner. The owner's successful receipt names the request, the retract transaction, the value that was locked, the recipient and the returned output. The tip slot against the deadline slots decides the window, never the host clock. After the window closes the refusal says the request can no longer be taken back, and the request stays pending. Updates and deletions cannot be retracted; insertions and terminal witnesses can. The root stays where it was.
open-datum insert books a new request after reclaim.
open-datum fold folds it, and an independent inspection reads active.

A closed registry is booted with open-datum create --closed ..., which pins the closed-datum application whose payload is written once. Every later command follows the registry's mode with no further flag, and open-datum update on a closed registry stops before anything is built or signed, saying the registry is closed. The project rehearses that scene on a development node on every change, in the hosted job "Closed-datum journey from the release archive".

when-a-command-stops.text: A command that stops prints why, in one outcome class with its own exit status. Status 2 is a mistake on the command line.

partial-outcomes-and-recovery.text: Every submission is journalled in your state directory before it is sent, and its confirmation after. A command never resubmits, reboots or overwrites on its own:

partial names what was left behind. An insertion of a key the registry already holds is booked by the application and then cannot be folded: the receipt names the pending request, and its deposit stays locked in it. A fold that is asked for after its request's deadline, or that the registry cannot take, is a client-refusal that submitted nothing; the request stays pending.

timeout names the submitted transaction when its confirmation did not arrive within --confirm-timeout seconds (default 600). The entry stays unresolved, and every later write on that registry refuses until inspect resolves it from the chain.
inspect is the recovery: it reads the journal, checks each unresolved submission against the chain, and advances the saved state only for what the chain shows.
A second create on the same directory is refused, including one that was held while another create finished.

on-a-public-network.text: The same ordinary commands use a Koios API on the requested test network. Three settings change: the Koios base URL, the network magic and the optional token file. The preprod runbook gives the faucet funding, the amounts, the waits and every step with real values, and says which parts of it have run on preprod and which have not.

A preview shows what a write would cost before you sign anything. It names the caller by an enterprise address instead of a signing key, reads through a connection that cannot sign or send, and writes nothing: your state directory is byte for byte the same afterwards.

The preview receipt names the wallet outputs it selects, each body's fee, the execution units the local evaluator measured for each script, the total collateral each states and the collateral it returns, a digest of the protocol parameters it was built under, and the outlay: the fee, the value the booking locks and a bound on the fold that follows. An insertion or a termination is two transactions, and the fold exists only once its booking has confirmed, so the preview bounds the fold from the network's parameters. A preview is not a confirmation: its bodies are built for one moment.

insert, update, terminate and fold take --fund-input TXID#IX, the wallet output that funds and collateralises the write, and --max-outlay LOVELACE. A booking, an update or a fold past the outlay is not signed. Without --fund-input, a write spends the wallet's largest ada-only output and returns the change. A fee is never declared: the booking's units are measured on the body that will be submitted. A funding output that cannot leave a return of at least its minimum ada is refused before anything is submitted.

what-the-project-runs-on-its-own.text: What the project runs on its own.

Two further tools ship in this archive, and they are not part of the path above. They are run by the project against a registry that already exists, and they need things an ordinary user does not have, so no step here uses them.

cli-controls (built from conformance#cli-controls) attaches to an existing registry with a fresh key and rehearses four refusals, each beside the ordinary command that does the same thing legitimately: an update another wallet's signature stands for, a release outside any fold, a second insertion of an active key and an insertion of a terminal key. It also requires --node-socket for a separate independent probe of the chain, and it keeps key files. That socket is never given to singular or open-datum.

tools/demo1_readback.sh reads one key's token output back from Koios by policy id and asset name alone, and compares the output reference, the inline datum bytes and their hash with an open-datum inspect receipt. It exits 0 only when the indexer finds exactly one output holding the token and agrees with the inspect, within --max-lag slots of its tip. Run it from the extracted archive with --provider koios; it is the check the preprod runbook uses after steps 5 and 7.
Both are described in the reviewer's map.

what-this-does-not-claim.text: The open-datum application protects the payload and the deposit, nothing more; it is a demonstration of the registry's mechanics. This page and its receipts are evidence of behaviour on a private development node only. Public-network receipts are on the preprod runbook, with their limits; nor is any complete conformance claimed here.
